question: Which two advanced linked list types are covered in Week 4?
options: Sorted linked lists and doubly linked lists
Circular linked lists and skip lists
Stacks and queues implemented with linked lists
Hash-based linked lists and binary trees
correctAnswer: Sorted linked lists and doubly linked lists
explanation: Week 4 covers sorted linked lists and doubly linked lists.

question: What is a sorted linked list?
options: A list whose elements always stay in the order they were inserted, like a classic linked list
A list that keeps its elements in a specific order (e.g. numerical or alphabetical) at all times
A list that is sorted once, only when it is printed, and left unsorted the rest of the time
A list that copies its elements into an array so they can be sorted quickly using binary search
correctAnswer: A list that keeps its elements in a specific order (e.g. numerical or alphabetical) at all times
explanation: Unlike regular linked lists that keep insertion order, sorted linked lists always maintain a predetermined sequence.

question: Short answer: What is the primary benefit of a sorted linked list?
options: It uses less memory than an array, since sorted data can be stored in fewer bytes per node
Reads become O(1), because the position of every element can be calculated from its value
Data is always sorted, so you can access it in sorted order without extra sorting operations
It never needs traversal, because the smallest and largest values are always at the two ends
correctAnswer: Data is always sorted, so you can access it in sorted order without extra sorting operations
explanation: Sorted linked lists are useful when elements are frequently accessed, searched or retrieved in sorted order.

question: Fill in the blank: Insertions into a sorted linked list automatically place elements in their _____ according to the sorting criteria.
options: original insertion position
head position
tail position
appropriate position
correctAnswer: appropriate position
explanation: Each insert goes where it belongs so the order is always maintained.

question: Sorted insertion: when should the new node be inserted at the BEGINNING of the list?
options: When the list is empty or the new data is smaller than the head's data
When the new data is larger than the tail's data, so it belongs at the very front
Always; sorted lists insert at the beginning and re-sort afterwards
When the new data equals the tail's data, to keep duplicates together
correctAnswer: When the list is empty or the new data is smaller than the head's data
explanation: In that case set newNode->next = head, update head to the new node, and return it.

question: Sorted insertion: while traversing to find the insertion position, when do you keep moving to the next node?
options: While the current node's data is greater than the new data being inserted
While the next node exists and its data is less than the new data
Until you reach the tail, regardless of what data each node contains
While the next node is NULL and its data is smaller than the new data
correctAnswer: While the next node exists and its data is less than the new data
explanation: Stop when there's no next node or the next node's data is >= the new data, then insert after current.

question: Sorted insertion: once the right 'current' node is found, how is the new node inserted?
options: newNode->next = NULL; current->next = newNode;
current->next = newNode; newNode->next = current->next;
newNode->next = current->next; current->next = newNode;
newNode->next = current; current->next = newNode->next;
correctAnswer: newNode->next = current->next; current->next = newNode;
explanation: Set the new node's link first. Doing it in the other order would make newNode point to itself and lose the rest of the list.

question: A sorted linked list contains 10 -> 20 -> 40. After inserting 30 and then 5, what is the list?
explanation: 30 goes between 20 and 40; 5 is smaller than the head so it becomes the new head.

question: Coding: Which SortedInsert is correct (sorted by StudentId, ascending)?
options: Student* SortedInsert(Student* head, int id, int age) { Student* n = CreateNewNode(id, age); if (head == NULL || id < head->StudentId) { n->NextStudent = head; return n; } Student* cur = head; while (cur->NextStudent != NULL && cur->NextStudent->StudentId < id) cur = cur->NextStudent; n->NextStudent = cur->NextStudent; cur->NextStudent = n; return head; }

Student* SortedInsert(Student* head, int id, int age) { Student* n = CreateNewNode(id, age); if (head == NULL || id < head->StudentId) { n->NextStudent = head; return n; } Student* cur = head; while (cur->NextStudent != NULL && cur->NextStudent->StudentId < id) cur = cur->NextStudent; cur->NextStudent = n; n->NextStudent = cur->NextStudent; return head; }

Student* SortedInsert(Student* head, int id, int age) { Student* n = CreateNewNode(id, age); if (head == NULL || id < head->StudentId) { n->NextStudent = head; return n; } Student* cur = head; while (cur->NextStudent != NULL && cur->NextStudent->StudentId > id) cur = cur->NextStudent; n->NextStudent = cur->NextStudent; cur->NextStudent = n; return head; }

Student* SortedInsert(Student* head, int id, int age) { Student* n = CreateNewNode(id, age); if (head == NULL || id < head->StudentId) { n->NextStudent = head; return n; } Student* cur = head; while (cur != NULL && cur->NextStudent != NULL && cur->StudentId < id) cur = cur->NextStudent; n->NextStudent = cur->NextStudent; cur->NextStudent = n; return head; }
correctAnswer: Student* SortedInsert(Student* head, int id, int age) { Student* n = CreateNewNode(id, age); if (head == NULL || id < head->StudentId) { n->NextStudent = head; return n; } Student* cur = head; while (cur->NextStudent != NULL && cur->NextStudent->StudentId < id) cur = cur->NextStudent; n->NextStudent = cur->NextStudent; cur->NextStudent = n; return head; }
explanation: It follows the four steps: create the node, handle empty or smaller-than-head, traverse while the NEXT node is smaller, then link. Swapping the last two link lines makes the new node point to itself and loses the rest of the list; comparing with > stops in the wrong place; comparing cur instead of cur->NextStudent inserts one node too late (e.g. 30 lands after 40).

question: What makes a doubly linked list different from a classic linked list?
options: Each node stores two copies of its value, so data can be recovered if one copy is lost
Each node has two links (next and previous), and the list tracks both the first and last nodes
It has two head pointers, one for even-indexed nodes and one for odd-indexed nodes
Each node links to the next two nodes so traversal can skip ahead
correctAnswer: Each node has two links (next and previous), and the list tracks both the first and last nodes
explanation: A doubly linked list has next and previous links and keeps track of the head and tail.

question: Short answer: What can a doubly linked list do that a classic (singly) linked list cannot?
options: Store more than one value per node, since each node has room for a second data field
Read any element in O(1), because the tail pointer lets it jump straight to any index
Move both forward and backward, including starting at the last node and working back to the first
Insert at the beginning in O(1), which a singly linked list can't do
correctAnswer: Move both forward and backward, including starting at the last node and working back to the first
explanation: A classic list only moves forward because no node knows its previous node.

question: Reverse iteration in a doubly linked list is useful for which of these?
options: Binary search, since the list can be entered from both ends at once
Removing the need for a head pointer, since the tail is always known
Making reads O(1) by approaching each index from the closer end
Processing data in reverse sequence or reversing the list itself
correctAnswer: Processing data in reverse sequence or reversing the list itself
explanation: Reverse traversal helps when data must be processed backwards or for algorithms like reversing the list.

question: With a tail pointer maintained, what is the time complexity of inserting or deleting at the END of a doubly linked list?
options: O(N)
O(log N)
explanation: This is tail pointer optimization: you can jump straight to the tail instead of traversing.

question: Which is NOT listed as a use case for doubly linked lists?
options: Undo/redo functionality in text editors
O(1) random access by index
Dequeues (double-ended queues)
Caches that move frequently accessed items to the front
correctAnswer: O(1) random access by index
explanation: Doubly linked lists still need traversal to reach an index. Their listed use cases are undo/redo, caches and dequeues.

question: Fill in the blank: Even with bidirectional traversal, reading or searching a doubly linked list is _____.
options: O(log N)
O(N)
correctAnswer: O(N)
explanation: The exact memory location of a node still isn't known, so the computer must traverse.

question: Which struct correctly represents a doubly linked list Student node?
options: typedef struct Student { int StudentId; int Age; struct Student* NextStudent; struct Student** PreviousStudent; } Student;
typedef struct Student { int StudentId; int Age; struct Student* NextStudent; } Student;
typedef struct Student { int StudentId; int Age; struct Student NextStudent; struct Student PreviousStudent; } Student;
typedef struct Student { int StudentId; int Age; struct Student* NextStudent; struct Student* PreviousStudent; } Student;
correctAnswer: typedef struct Student { int StudentId; int Age; struct Student* NextStudent; struct Student* PreviousStudent; } Student;
explanation: A doubly linked node needs pointers to both the next and previous Student.

question: In the doubly linked CreateNewNode, what are NextStudent and PreviousStudent set to, and who sets their real values?
options: Both set to NULL; it's the calling function's responsibility to populate them
Both set to the head; CreateNewNode handles all of the linking itself
Left uninitialized, since insert functions overwrite them anyway
Next set to NULL and Previous set to the tail, so it's ready to append at the end
correctAnswer: Both set to NULL; it's the calling function's responsibility to populate them
explanation: The helper just creates a clean node; insert functions do the linking.

question: In the doubly linked InsertAtBeginning, which statements are needed (assuming head is not NULL)?
options: newStudent->PreviousStudent = head; head->NextStudent = newStudent; return head;
newStudent->NextStudent = head; head->PreviousStudent = newStudent; return newStudent;
newStudent->NextStudent = head; newStudent->PreviousStudent = head; return newStudent;
newStudent->NextStudent = head; head->PreviousStudent = newStudent; return head->NextStudent;
correctAnswer: newStudent->NextStudent = head; head->PreviousStudent = newStudent; return newStudent;
explanation: The old head's PreviousStudent (previously NULL) now points to the new node, and the new node's next points to the old head.

question: Short answer: Why must the doubly linked InsertAtBeginning check whether head is NULL before setting head->PreviousStudent?
options: To keep the list sorted when the new node is smaller than the head
It doesn't need to; setting a NULL pointer's field is safely ignored
On an empty list, head is NULL, and dereferencing it would crash
To free the old head first, so its PreviousStudent can be reused for the new node
correctAnswer: On an empty list, head is NULL, and dereferencing it would crash
explanation: Guard with: if (head != NULL) head->PreviousStudent = newStudent;

question: In the doubly linked InsertAtEnd (traversing from head), which two links must be set once the tail is found?
options: tail->NextStudent = newStudent; newStudent->PreviousStudent = tail->PreviousStudent;
newStudent->NextStudent = head; head->PreviousStudent = newStudent;
tail->PreviousStudent = newStudent; newStudent->NextStudent = tail;
tail->NextStudent = newStudent; newStudent->PreviousStudent = tail;
correctAnswer: tail->NextStudent = newStudent; newStudent->PreviousStudent = tail;
explanation: The tail's next points to the new node, and the new node's previous points back to the tail.

question: How does FreeList for a doubly linked list compare to the classic version?
options: It is like the classic implementation: save next, free current, move on
It must walk backwards from the tail so that no PreviousStudent link is lost
It frees each node twice, once for each of its two links
It frees only the head, since freeing it releases every linked node
correctAnswer: It is like the classic implementation: save next, free current, move on
explanation: You only need to follow NextStudent links to free every node once.

question: InsertAtIndex: what should happen if the index is 0?
options: Return an error, since index 0 is reserved for the head
Call InsertAtBeginning, since a new head is being created
Call InsertAtEnd, because the list may be empty at that point
Traverse to index -1 first, then link the new node after it as usual
correctAnswer: Call InsertAtBeginning, since a new head is being created
explanation: Index 0 means the new node becomes the head.

question: InsertAtIndex: to which position do you traverse before inserting?
options: index + 1
index
index - 1
the tail node
correctAnswer: index - 1
explanation: Traverse until current is NULL or index - 1 iterations are done, so current is the node BEFORE the insertion point.

question: InsertAtIndex: What is the correct order of the four link updates (with current at index - 1)?
options: 1) new->Previous = current->Previous; 2) new->Next = current; 3) current->Previous = new; 4) current->Previous->Next = new
1) current->Next = new; 2) new->Next = current->Next; 3) if current->Next != NULL, current->Next->Previous = new; 4) new->Previous = current
1) new->Next = current->Next; 2) current->Next = new; 3) if new->Next != NULL, current->Previous = new; 4) new->Previous = current
1) new->Next = current->Next; 2) if current->Next != NULL, current->Next->Previous = new; 3) current->Next = new; 4) new->Previous = current
correctAnswer: 1) new->Next = current->Next; 2) if current->Next != NULL, current->Next->Previous = new; 3) current->Next = new; 4) new->Previous = current
explanation: You must use current->Next to wire the new node BEFORE overwriting current->Next; otherwise you lose the rest of the list.

question: In InsertAtIndex, why check 'if current->NextStudent is not NULL' before updating its PreviousStudent?
options: Because inserting at the end means there is no next node to update
It isn't necessary, because NULL->PreviousStudent is simply ignored
To keep the list sorted when the new node has the largest value
Because a NULL next node means the list is empty, so the head must be updated instead
correctAnswer: Because inserting at the end means there is no next node to update
explanation: If current is the tail, current->NextStudent is NULL and dereferencing it would crash.

question: Doubly linked list: A <-> B <-> C. After InsertAtIndex(head, 1, X), what is B->PreviousStudent?
options: A
X
NULL
C
correctAnswer: X
explanation: X is inserted between A and B, giving A <-> X <-> B <-> C, so B's previous is X.

question: Coding: Which function correctly prints a doubly linked list in REVERSE, given its tail?
options: void PrintReverse(Student* tail) { Student* cur = tail; while (cur->PreviousStudent != NULL) { printf("%d ", cur->StudentId); cur = cur->PreviousStudent; } }
void PrintReverse(Student* tail) { Student* cur = tail; while (cur != NULL) { printf("%d ", cur->StudentId); cur = cur->NextStudent; } }
void PrintReverse(Student* tail) { Student* cur = tail; while (cur != NULL) { printf("%d ", cur->StudentId); cur = cur->PreviousStudent; } }
void PrintReverse(Student* tail) { Student* cur = tail; while (cur != NULL) { cur = cur->PreviousStudent; printf("%d ", cur->StudentId); } }
correctAnswer: void PrintReverse(Student* tail) { Student* cur = tail; while (cur != NULL) { printf("%d ", cur->StudentId); cur = cur->PreviousStudent; } }
explanation: Start at the tail and follow PreviousStudent until NULL. Following NextStudent from the tail prints only the tail; stopping at cur->PreviousStudent != NULL skips the head; moving before printing skips the tail and dereferences NULL at the end.

question: Coding: Which correctly deletes a middle node 'target' from a doubly linked list (target has both a previous and a next node)?
options: target->PreviousStudent->NextStudent = target->NextStudent; target->NextStudent->PreviousStudent = target->PreviousStudent; target = NULL;
target->PreviousStudent->NextStudent = target->NextStudent; target->NextStudent->PreviousStudent = target->NextStudent; free(target);
free(target); target->PreviousStudent->NextStudent = target->NextStudent; target->NextStudent->PreviousStudent = target->PreviousStudent;
target->PreviousStudent->NextStudent = target->NextStudent; target->NextStudent->PreviousStudent = target->PreviousStudent; free(target);
correctAnswer: target->PreviousStudent->NextStudent = target->NextStudent; target->NextStudent->PreviousStudent = target->PreviousStudent; free(target);
explanation: Both neighbours are re-linked to bypass the target, then it's freed. Setting the next node's PreviousStudent to target->NextStudent breaks the back link; freeing first means the later lines read freed memory; target = NULL instead of free() leaks the node.
